13267: They are Gentiles (and perhaps scattered Israelites) gathered into one flock under Israel's shepherd, fulfilling Ezekiel's promise; the image is of enlargement, not replacement (Keener, Bauckham).
13268: Lazarus raised and the plan to kill Jesus
13269: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, is ill. Jesus, who loves them, deliberately waits two days, and Lazarus dies. When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets him with faith and grief; Jesus says, 'I am the resurrection and the life', and she confesses him as Messiah and Son of God. Mary weeps at his feet, and Jesus, deeply moved and angry at death, weeps too. At the tomb he prays and calls, 'Lazarus, come out!' The dead man comes out bound in grave clothes. Many believe. The chief priests and Pharisees fear the Romans will destroy 'our place and our nation'. Caiaphas says it is better that one man die for the people, which John calls an unwitting prophecy that Jesus would die to gather God's scattered children. From that day they plan to kill him.
13270: In Mark the temple action triggers the plot against Jesus; in John it is the raising of Lazarus, the seventh and greatest sign. The leaders' fear (John 11:48) was realistic: Roman authorities did crush messianic movements, and by the time John wrote, Rome had in fact destroyed the temple and city in AD 70. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; an ornate ossuary (bone box) inscribed with the name 'Joseph son of Caiaphas', found in Jerusalem in 1990, may belong to his family.
13271: Jewish burial happened quickly, usually the same day, in a rock-cut tomb sealed with a stone. The body was washed, wrapped in cloths, with the face covered by a separate cloth. Mourning lasted seven days (shiva), and friends came to comfort the family; professional mourners might wail. Later rabbinic tradition said the soul lingered near the body for three days, so by the fourth day death was certain and decay had begun ('he stinks', John 11:39). Jesus' delay means no one could say Lazarus was merely unconscious.
13272:
Martha voices the faith of many Jews, especially Pharisees: 'I know he will rise in the resurrection on the last day' (John 11:24, compare Dan 12:2). Jesus answers that the resurrection life of the last day is present in him now. The scene echoes Ezekiel's promise, 'I will open your graves... and you shall know that I am the Lord' (Ezek 37:12-13).

Caiaphas thinks politically: one man's death to save the nation from Rome. John sees in it Israel's hope of restoration: Jesus would die 'not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad' (John 11:52), the language of the ingathering of exiles (Isa 43:5-7, Ezek 37:21).
13273: Readers who had buried believers would hear Jesus' promise to Martha as their own. They would also see that Jesus' own people included those who loved him (Martha, Mary, Lazarus and the many 'Jews' who came to comfort them and believed, John 11:45).
13274: Jesus does not hurry past grief; he weeps beside it, and he is angry at death. Resurrection hope is not only for the end; the life of the age to come meets people in their losses now.
13275: God opens Israel's graves and gives his Spirit.
13276: Many who sleep in the dust will awake.
13278: God will swallow up death and wipe away tears.
13279: Gathering God's scattered children from the ends of the earth.
13280: 'The Jews' plotted Jesus' death as a people.
13281: Many Jews mourned with Martha and Mary and believed (John 11:45); the decision was taken by a small leadership circle fearing Rome (John 11:47-53).
13282: Anointed, welcomed as king, and the hour has come
13283: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany, Mary anoints Jesus' feet with expensive perfumed oil and wipes them with her hair; Judas objects, and Jesus says she has kept it for his burial. The next day crowds with palm branches greet Jesus, shouting 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel', and Jesus rides a young donkey. Some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he announces, 'The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified': like a grain of wheat, he must die to bear fruit. A voice from heaven answers his prayer. When lifted up, he will draw all people to himself. The narrator explains the unbelief of many with Isaiah, and notes that many leaders believed but did not confess it, fearing being put out of the synagogue. Jesus' final public appeal: 'I have come as light into the world.'
13284: This chapter ends the 'Book of Signs'. The second aposynagōgos passage (John 12:42-43) explicitly names rulers who believed secretly because of the Pharisees, 'for they loved human glory more than the glory of God'. The arrival of Greeks marks the turning point: when Gentiles seek Jesus, his 'hour' arrives. Scholars note that John's audience included such Gentile seekers.
13285: Nard was an imported perfume from India; a pound worth 300 denarii was almost a year's wages for a labourer. Letting down her hair in public was a startling, intimate act. Palm branches were symbols of Jewish national victory; they had been waved when Simon Maccabeus liberated Jerusalem and appeared on coins of the Jewish revolts against Rome. 'Hosanna' (Hebrew 'save, please') comes from Psalm 118, sung at Passover and Sukkot. To welcome someone into the city with palms was to greet a liberating king.
13286:
The crowd's cry is Ps 118:25-26, and John adds Zech 9:9: 'Do not fear, daughter of Zion; see, your king is coming, seated on a donkey's colt.' Zechariah's king comes humble and brings peace to the nations — not the warrior many hoped for. The 'lifting up' that will draw all people echoes Isaiah's servant who will be 'lifted up and greatly exalted' (Isa 52:13).

John quotes Isa 53:1 ('Lord, who has believed our report?') and Isa 6:10 (hardened eyes and hearts), and says Isaiah 'saw his glory' (John 12:41) — identifying the glory Isaiah saw on the throne with Jesus. Unbelief is explained within Israel's own prophetic story, not as a sign that Israel is rejected; Isaiah himself spoke of a people slow to see.
13287: A community that wondered why so many of their own people did not believe would find an answer in Isaiah: prophets had always met resistance. Secret believers would feel the sting of 12:43 and be urged to choose God's glory over human approval.
13288: Mary's lavish love, the humble king on a donkey, and the grain that must die all point to the same truth: in John, glory is love giving itself away. Fear of losing social standing remains a powerful reason people hide what they believe.
13289: 'Save us... blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'
13290: Your king comes humble, on a donkey.
13291: The servant lifted up and exalted.
13293: Eyes blinded and hearts hardened; Isaiah sees the Lord's glory.
13294: Washing feet and the new commandment
13295: Before Passover, knowing his hour has come and 'having loved his own... he loved them to the end', Jesus rises from supper, wraps a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet. Peter refuses, then asks for a full bath; Jesus says unless he washes him, Peter has no share with him. Jesus tells them to wash one another's feet as he has done. Troubled, he announces that one of them will betray him; the Beloved Disciple, reclining next to Jesus, asks who, and Jesus gives a morsel to Judas, who goes out — 'and it was night'. Jesus says the Son of Man is now glorified, gives a new commandment, 'love one another as I have loved you', and predicts that Peter will deny him three times.
13296: Here the 'Book of Glory' begins. The Beloved Disciple appears for the first time by that title (John 13:23). John dates the supper 'before the feast of Passover' (John 13:1) and Jesus' death on the day of preparation, when Passover lambs were slaughtered (John 19:14), while the Synoptics present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. Scholars have proposed different solutions: different calendars in use, John's theological choice to align Jesus' death with the lambs, or the Synoptic account being a Passover-like meal held early. John has no institution of bread and cup; the foot washing stands in its place.
13297: Guests reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, feet stretched away; the disciple 'at Jesus' bosom' was in a place of honour and intimacy. Feet were dusty from roads, and washing them was the job of the lowest servant; Jewish sources suggest even a Jewish slave should not be required to do it. A host might offer water, but would not wash guests' feet himself. A teacher washing his students' feet was a shocking reversal of honour.
13298:
Jesus, knowing that 'the Father had given all things into his hands' (John 13:3), uses that authority to serve. The scene resembles the servant of Isaiah who humbles himself. Hospitality in Israel's stories begins with water for feet (Gen 18:4). Judas's betrayal fulfils Ps 41:9, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me' — the betrayal by a table companion, a deep breach of covenant friendship.

The 'new commandment' is not new in content — 'love your neighbour as yourself' is Lev 19:18 — but new in its measure: 'as I have loved you'. It is the covenant love of the new covenant community (Jer 31:31-34), marked out as Jesus' disciples by their love.
13299: A small, pressured community needed the foot-washing more than a doctrine: humility, forgiveness and practical care for one another. Readers who had seen betrayal and failure within the group would hear that even Judas sat at the table and Peter would fall — and that Jesus' love was 'to the end'.
13300: Leadership in the church is measured by the towel. The mark of Jesus' followers is not first their doctrine or culture but their love for one another, which outsiders can see.
13301: The friend who ate my bread lifted his heel against me.
13303: Abraham offers water to wash his guests' feet.
13304: The servant pours out his life.
13305: The 'new commandment' replaces the Old Testament law of love with a new Christian ethic.
13306: Love of neighbour is already Torah (Lev 19:18); what is new is the pattern and power of Jesus' self-giving love in the new covenant community (Keener, Thompson).
13307: The Father's house, the way, and the promised Advocate
13308: Jesus tells his troubled disciples to trust God and trust him. In his Father's house are many dwelling places; he goes to prepare a place and will come back to take them to himself. Thomas asks the way; Jesus says, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.' Philip asks to see the Father; Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises 'another Advocate' (Paraclete), the Spirit of truth, who will remain with them and teach them. He will not leave them orphans. If anyone loves him and keeps his word, the Father and he will come and make their home with that person. He gives them peace, 'not as the world gives', and says, 'Rise, let us go from here.'
13309: Chapters 14-17 are the 'Farewell Discourse'. 'Rise, let us go from here' (John 14:31) followed by three more chapters of speech is one of the clues for the theory that the Gospel was edited in stages (Brown), though others see it as a deliberate literary move or a walk toward Gethsemane (Carson). The promise of the Spirit to 'remind' them of everything Jesus said (John 14:26) is also a statement about how this Gospel understood its own remembering and interpreting of Jesus.
13310: The farewell speech was a recognised Jewish genre: Jacob blesses his sons (Gen 49), Moses gives Deuteronomy before his death, David instructs Solomon (1 Kgs 2:1-9), and later Jewish 'testaments' (such as the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs) follow a pattern: announcement of departure, comfort, commands to love, warnings, promises, and appointment of successors. A paraclete in legal settings was an advocate or helper who stood beside someone. A 'house' with many rooms suggests a large extended-family household, where married sons added rooms around a shared courtyard.
13311:
'My Father's house' in John 2:16 is the temple. In the temple there were many rooms (1 Kgs 6:5, Ezek 40:17) and the hope of dwelling in God's house was the hope of Psalm 23:6 and Psalm 27:4. The same word for 'dwelling place' (monē) returns in John 14:23, where the Father and Son come to dwell with the believer. So the promise is God's presence: the household of the Father, now and at Jesus' return.

'Way', 'truth' and 'life' are rich Hebrew words. The way (derek) is how one walks in Torah (Ps 119:30); truth (emet) is God's faithfulness; life is covenant blessing (Deut 30:15-20). Moses asked to see God's glory (Exod 33:18); Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus says he has been seen in the Son. The Spirit as 'another Advocate' continues Jesus' presence as Joshua continued Moses' leadership (Deut 34:9).
13312: A community that had lost the eyewitnesses (the Beloved Disciple had died, John 21:23) and lived without Jesus' physical presence would hear: you are not orphans; the Spirit remains and teaches; the Father and Son make their home with you.
13313: The famous verse 14:6 is said to anxious friends, not to opponents. It invites us to know God as Father through Jesus. The home Jesus prepares is above all a relationship — being where he is.
13314: Dwelling in the house of the Lord forever.
13315: Moses asks to see God's glory.
13316: Moses' farewell: do not fear, God will not leave you.
13317: 'I have chosen the way of faithfulness.'
13318: My dwelling place shall be with them.
13319: Jesus promises each believer a 'mansion' in heaven after death, and 14:6 is mainly a verdict on other religions.
13320: 'Dwelling places' are rooms in the Father's household (compare 14:23: God dwelling with us now), with a future hope too; 14:6 is comfort to disciples about knowing the Father through Jesus, though its exclusive claim is debated in its implications (Carson, Keener, Köstenberger).
13321: The true vine and the friends of Jesus
13322: Jesus says, 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the vine-grower.' Branches that bear fruit are pruned; branches cut off wither. The disciples are to remain (abide) in him as he remains in them, for apart from him they can do nothing. As the Father loved him, he has loved them; they are to remain in his love by keeping his commands, so that his joy may be in them. The greatest love is to lay down one's life for one's friends. 'I no longer call you servants... I have called you friends.' He chose them to bear lasting fruit. The world will hate them as it hated him; but the Advocate and they themselves will testify about him.
13323: The Farewell Discourse continues, perhaps on the walk to the Mount of Olives. The warning that the world will hate the disciples would match the experience of John's community: rejection by neighbours, by some in the synagogue, and possibly suspicion from Roman authorities, as believers would not join in civic and imperial cults. Some scholars see chapters 15-17 as an expanded second edition of the farewell material.
13324: Vineyards were everywhere in the land of Israel. Pruning in late winter cut away dead and unfruitful wood so the vine would bear more; prunings were burned. 'Friend of the king' was a recognised court title in the ancient world for a trusted insider, and in Greco-Roman thought friendship meant frankness and shared counsel, unlike the relationship of master and slave, who is simply told what to do. Jesus elevates his followers to the status of confidants.
13325:
Israel was God's vine or vineyard: 'You brought a vine out of Egypt' (Ps 80:8-16); Isaiah's song of the vineyard grieves that it produced wild grapes (Isa 5:1-7); Jeremiah calls Israel a choice vine that went wild (Jer 2:21). A golden vine decorated the entrance to Herod's temple, as Josephus describes. When Jesus calls himself 'the true vine', he is not discarding Israel but presenting himself as the faithful Israel in whom God's people are rooted. To remain in him is to belong to God's people.

Abraham and Moses were called friends of God (Isa 41:8, Exod 33:11). Jesus extends that covenant intimacy to all his disciples: they know what the master is doing.
13326: A minority under pressure needed to hear that their identity rested on staying connected to Jesus and to one another in love, that fruit would come through pruning, and that being hated did not mean being abandoned.
13327: Christian life is not mainly effort but connection — remaining in a relationship of love. The status of 'friend' changes how believers relate to God: not as anxious servants but as trusted companions.
13328: Israel the vine brought out of Egypt.
13329: The song of the unfruitful vineyard.
13332: God speaks to Moses face to face, as with a friend.
13333: The vine replaces Israel: the church is the new vine and Israel has been cut off.
13334: Jesus is the faithful Israel-vine and his followers, Jewish and Gentile, are branches in him; the image is of fulfilment and belonging rather than rejection (Keener, Thompson, Bauckham).
13335: Grief turned to joy and the coming Spirit
13336: Jesus warns that his disciples will be put out of synagogues, and some will even think that killing them is service to God. It is better for them that he goes away, because then the Advocate will come, who will convict the world about sin, righteousness and judgement, and will guide the disciples into all truth. In 'a little while' they will not see him, and then they will see him again. Their grief will turn to joy, as a woman's labour pain gives way to joy at a birth. They will ask the Father in Jesus' name, for the Father himself loves them. The disciples say they now understand; Jesus warns they will be scattered, yet 'take heart; I have overcome the world'.
13337: John 16:2 is the third aposynagōgos passage and the most severe: exclusion and even killing. Scholars debate what this reflects. Martyn read it as the community's experience of formal expulsion; others note local tensions, the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7) and Paul's own earlier persecution of believers as a zealous Jew (Gal 1:13-14), and possible denunciation to Roman authorities. Reinhartz and others caution that we cannot simply read the community's history off the text. What is clear is that John's readers had suffered real loss and fear.
13338: Labour in childbirth was a common Jewish picture for the painful arrival of God's new age — the 'birth pangs of the Messiah'. In court, an advocate who 'convicts' brings evidence that shows who is truly in the wrong. Praying 'in the name' of someone meant praying as their representative, with their authority and character.
13339:
The woman in labour echoes Isaiah's images of Zion giving birth to a new people (Isa 26:17-19, Isa 66:7-14), where birth and resurrection are linked. Those who think persecuting others is 'service to God' (latreia, worship) stand in a line of zeal for God that Paul himself once embodied; the Gospel does not mock their zeal but calls it misdirected.

The Spirit guiding into 'all truth' recalls God's promise to put his Spirit within Israel so they would walk in his ways (Ezek 36:27) and the new covenant where all will know the Lord (Jer 31:34). The disciples' 'scattering' recalls Zech 13:7, 'strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered'.
13340: For believers who had been expelled, threatened or bereaved, this chapter named their pain honestly and promised joy that no one could take away. It also told them their suffering was foreseen, not a sign that God had abandoned them.
13341: Grief is not denied but transformed, like labour into birth. The Spirit continues Jesus' teaching presence. And the chapter warns religious people of every tradition, including Christians, that violence done 'for God' can be deeply mistaken.
13342: Labour pains and the dead rising.
13343: Zion gives birth; rejoicing replaces grief.
13344: Strike the shepherd, the sheep scatter.
13345: God's law written within; all will know the Lord.
13346: John 16:2 shows that Jews were persecutors of Christians, so Christians are always the innocent victims.
13347: It reflects a specific, painful local conflict within the Jewish family; within a few centuries the power relationship reversed and Christians persecuted Jews. The text warns all who think violence is worship (Brown, Reinhartz, Levine).
13348: Jesus' prayer: knowing God and being one
13349: Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven: 'Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you.' He defines eternal life: 'that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.' He has made the Father's name known to those the Father gave him. He prays for them: that they be kept in the Father's name, protected from the evil one, made holy in the truth, and sent into the world as he was sent. Then he prays for those who will believe through their word: that all may be one, as the Father is in him and he in the Father, so that the world may believe; and that they may be with him and see his glory, and that the Father's love may be in them.
13350: Since the sixteenth-century Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus, this has been called the 'High Priestly Prayer'. It concludes the Farewell Discourse. Its concern for unity probably reflects a community that faced divisions; the letters of John speak of members who 'went out from us' (1 John 2:19). It is also the clearest single statement of John's theology of knowing God.
13351: Lifting the eyes to heaven was a common Jewish posture in prayer. In Jewish thought a 'name' stood for the person's character and presence; God put his name in the temple (Deut 12:11). To be 'kept in the name' meant to be held within God's own presence and protection.
13352:
'Knowing God' in the Hebrew Bible is covenant relationship, not information: the new covenant promises that 'they shall all know me' (Jer 31:34), and Hosea mourns that there is 'no knowledge of God in the land' (Hos 4:1). Jesus defines eternal life — the life of the age to come — as that relational knowing (John 17:3), and holds firmly to Jewish monotheism: 'the only true God'.

Jesus prays like a high priest interceding for the people, consecrating himself (hagiazō) as priests and sacrifices were consecrated (Exod 28:41). His prayer that his followers be 'one' echoes the Shema's oneness (Deut 6:4) and Ezekiel's hope that God's scattered people would be gathered into one (Ezek 37:22). The glory he had 'before the world existed' links back to the Word in the beginning.
13353: A small, divided, pressured community would hear itself prayed for by name: kept, protected, consecrated and sent. Later believers ('those who will believe through their word') are also included in the prayer.
13354: Christianity at its heart is knowing God as Father through Jesus. The unity Jesus prays for is a relational unity of love modelled on God himself, and it is meant to be visible to the world.
13355: All shall know me, from least to greatest.
13356: God desires the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
13357: The Lord our God, the Lord is one.
13359: One nation, one king, no longer divided.
13360: 'Eternal life' in John 17 means going to heaven forever, and unity means one institutional church or simply invisible spiritual unity.
13361: Eternal life is defined as knowing God now (John 17:3); unity is a visible relational oneness of love that the world can see (Thompson, Bauckham, Keener).
13362: Arrest in the garden and the king before Pilate
13363: Jesus crosses the Kidron valley to a garden. Judas comes with a detachment of soldiers and temple police carrying lanterns and torches. Jesus asks whom they seek; when he says 'I am', they step back and fall to the ground. He asks them to let his disciples go. Peter cuts off the ear of Malchus, and Jesus tells him to put away his sword. Jesus is taken to Annas, former high priest, and questioned; meanwhile Peter, let into the courtyard through the Beloved Disciple's contact, denies Jesus three times by a charcoal fire. At dawn Jesus is taken to Pilate's headquarters; the accusers stay outside to avoid defilement before Passover. Pilate asks, 'Are you the king of the Jews?' Jesus says his kingdom is not from this world and that he came to testify to the truth. Pilate asks, 'What is truth?' and offers to release Jesus, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.
